summary:
Lethal violence against trans women in Rio Grande do Norte continued into 2026, after a year in which the state was recorded with no such killings at all. Two deaths are documented in the first half of the year, both of women killed inside their own homes.

In the early hours of 4 May 2026 Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, 27, was shot dead while she slept in the rented house she lived in on Rua Vivaldo Dantas, in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró, in western Rio Grande do Norte. Five men broke in. Military police found the body on a routine patrol. One suspect was arrested carrying a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. The state trans-rights association ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN publicly mourned her as an artist killed by the transphobia she faced.

A transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the municipality of Tibau do Sul on the state's southern coast, in late February 2026. She had been stabbed. The Civil Police opened an investigation, and ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN called for justice.

The state's recorded count has moved sharply. Rio Grande do Norte appeared with no recorded trans killings in 2024 in the ANTRA dossier and with four in the 2025 tabulation, the largest deterioration recorded for any state in that dataset. Both are raw counts, no per-capita figure for the state accompanies them, and a change of that size from a zero base therefore establishes no rate.

The zero counts carry limited weight on their own. The dossier behind them records systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, and one reproduction of the 2025 figures records no trans killings in Rio Grande do Norte for that year at all, contradicting the count of four given elsewhere. The two 2026 deaths post-date both tallies and are not yet reflected in any count for the state.

Sources document no rule of Rio Grande do Norte's own on the housing of trans prisoners. Custodial placement of LGBTI people arrested or imprisoned in the state stands under Brazil's federal framework, and no placement policy at state level appears in the sources consulted.
tangentialFactors:
Raw state rankings in the same dataset place Ceará and Minas Gerais at the top with eight killings each, with Paraíba alongside Rio Grande do Norte on four, and one macro-region, the Northeast, accounts for 38 of the year's total. Rankings of this kind are by raw count only; without per-capita denominators, a populous state's higher count and a small state's count do not compare as risk.

Figures for Brazil as a whole, and the federal rules on documents, health care and custody that apply in Rio Grande do Norte, are carried outside this state record.
localsOnly:
ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN is the local trans-rights association named in both 2026 cases, mourning Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta and calling for justice for Naomi. It is the only state-level trans advocacy body identified in the sources.

The Mossoró killing was found by the military police on patrol and one suspect is in custody; the Praia da Pipa killing is under investigation by the Civil Police. Neither case has a recorded outcome.

Residents have no reliable local count of lethal violence against trans people. Rio Grande do Norte was recorded with zero trans killings in 2024, then four for 2025 in one tabulation and zero in another, and the dossier's compilers attribute the zeros to official bodies failing to record LGBTQIA+ victims.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 state figures for Rio Grande do Norte are unresolved: one account gives four killings for the state, another reproduces the same dossier as recording none. No per-capita rate for the state is published against which either figure can be read.

Whether the 2026 killings in Mossoró and Tibau do Sul enter the next dossier cycle is not yet established.

Two sources consulted hold no rule specific to Rio Grande do Norte. One is Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil', which in its Politics section describes national prison arrangements, states that transgender people have the right to be called by their social name and to be sent to women's prisons, and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing, and footnotes a Mix Brasil report archived on 18 January 2012. The other is Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison', read on 28 September 2026, which records no trans-prisoner housing rule for Brazil or for Rio Grande do Norte and documents only vulnerability and stigma effects on travesti and transgender rehabilitation.

Figures for Brazil as a whole, and federal rules on documents, health care and custody, are not reproduced in this state record.
